- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model should not underestimate price; adjust forecast upward by 1–2% if price has not yet reacted to bullish sentiment.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and price is trending upward, model should not overestimate; reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid “overshoot after spikes.”  
- When official event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model should not ignore downward pressure; apply a 0.5–1.5% downward bias to forecast.  
- If model shows gradual upward trend (e.g., +0.05–0.10 per day) but true price spikes sharply, model likely underestimates event-driven volatility — add 0.5–1.0% to forecast at spike point.  
- If sentiment and price move in opposite directions (e.g., sentiment bullish, price falling), model may be misaligned — check for policy or auction events that override sentiment; adjust forecast to reflect event-driven override.  
- For 30-day horizon, if model shows mean reversion toward prior 10-day average, but true price deviates >3% from that average, model may be lagging — apply a 1–2% correction toward actual trend.
